transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-15
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Anika Rao (Kyronix Head of ML), Jorge Martinez (Kyronix Platform Eng), Sasha Cole (Kyronix CTO)
Links shared: https://redwood.app/kyronix/pilot/bench-20261114.xlsx, /shared/kyronix/trace-sample-11-14.json

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
- Reviewed week-over-week latency and throughput vs baseline provider (LexisAI)
- Noted 18-24% p99 latency gap on 8k token flows when cold KV cache; gap shrinks to ~6% with warm cache and batch tuning
- Discussed dedicated slot vs hosted routing for heavy tail requests and data residency concerns
- Agreed next steps: run 10k mixed-load with warm cache, share traces, security deep-dive next week

Topics flagged:
- Latency delta on long-context flows
- Throughput under sustained 500 RPS bursts
- KV cache effectiveness and cache-warming strategy
- Quantization/FP16 tradeoffs for quality vs unit-cost
- Network egress and VPC peering constraints

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: All right everyone thanks for joining, we're on the 11-15 pilot readout for Kyronix. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Anika: Hi this is Anika, sorry running late, Head of ML at Kyronix.
[00:12] Jorge: Jorge here, platform.
[00:14] Sasha: Sasha, CTO.
[00:17] Liam: Liam O'Neill from Redwood infra, hey all.
[00:19] Maya: Cool, ok agenda: run the week 2 bench vs your baseline, highlight the tails, propose tuning options. Liam will lead the numbers.

[00:28] Liam: Cool, jumping in. We did three runs friday through sunday, mixed workload: 60% chat-style convo, 30% short completions, 10% long-form (6–8k tokens). Baseline provider is LexisAI per the POC contract. A few headline numbers: median token latency is around parity, p95 is about 10–12% better on Redwood, p99 is where Lexis still has a lead on long-context cold-cache flows — roughly 18–24% depending on sequence length.
[01:05] Anika: Hm 18–24% p99, is that overall or only for the 8k jobs?
[01:10] Liam: Mostly the 6–8k token jobs. For 1–2k token flows we match or slightly beat Lexis, especially when the KV cache hit is warm.
[01:21] Jorge: When you say warm, you're talking about the prefix KV cache, right? Not OS cache.
[01:25] Liam: Right, KV cache. Our default point estimate: cold cache means extra decode overhead to refill KV and some kernel warmup. With a warm cache we saw p99 latency close to Lexis within ~6%.

[01:40] Maya: Can you explain where the extra ~12% is coming from in the cold case? Is it CPU scheduling, GPU kernel selection, or network egress?
[01:48] Liam: It's a mix. Our tracing shows two contributors: first, KV refill spikes go synchronous for the long tails - that'll show as additional 50–200ms per request for those long contexts. Second, kernel launch jitter on a subset of model sharding paths — when sequence lengths jump we sometimes hit a slower kernel path for the first few iterations. Network egress wasn't dominant on our cloud runs, but on your VPC-like network it could add 10–20ms if peering isn't optimal.

[02:25] Anika: Is that kernel path an artifact of quantization profiles? We're testing an 8-bit quantized variant right now.
[02:31] Liam: Good call. Yes, some quantized kernels fall back to slower code paths until the fast fused kernels are JIT'd for that pattern. For the 8-bit runs we did see a little more variance. We can try a warm-up batch to trigger the fast kernel earlier — that reduces variance.

[02:55] Sasha: On quality, Anika's worried about 8-bit regressions. Any measured quality delta vs Lexis for the 8-bit runs?
[03:03] Liam: We ran a small eval set — rouge/bertscore-style checks — and saw negligible deltas on the tasks Kyronix provided. But those were short tasks; we should expand to long-context QA to be sure.

[03:20] Jorge: Throughput — how did Redwood behave under sustained 500 RPS bursts? Lexis advertised a smoother degradation curve.
[03:27] Liam: We hammered a 500 RPS sustained burst for 30 minutes. Baseline sustained throughput was comparable. Our shedding policy kicked in earlier by design to protect latency SLOs; that explains some of the unit-cost differences. We can relax the shedding if you prefer throughput over latency for your use case.

[03:48] Maya: Can you quantify the cost/p95 tradeoff?
[03:51] Liam: Rough numbers: with conservative shedding and default batching we saw token unit cost ~12% lower than Lexis, with p95 latency 8–10% lower. If we disable shedding to match Lexis throughput, unit cost rises ~18% and p95 creeps toward parity. Those are ballpark pro-forma from our bench.

[04:14] Anika: So we have three levers: batch sizing, shedding threshold, and cache warming. Any recommendations for our production profile?
[04:21] Liam: For Kyronix — since you have frequent multi-turns and some very long flows — we recommend: 1) warm-start strategy for KV on known sessions, 2) slightly increase batch target for background short completions, 3) run a short pre-warm window for long-form jobs to force the fast kernels (Liam: we'll provide a script).

[04:44] Jorge: The warm-start script — do we need to change our client side, or can Redwood issue a prefetch call?
[04:50] Liam: Both are possible. Easiest is Redwood-issued warm-prefetch API (one-time hook) that primes KV from your last checkpoints. Alternative is client prefetch — a few lines. We'll provide both options.

[05:04] Maya: Quick sanity check — are there any security flags with prefetch in private deployments? Jorge?
[05:09] Jorge: Prefetch itself is fine if auth is maintained, but if prefetch writes into a shared cache we need namespacing — otherwise one customer's prefetch could affect another's warm-lane. Kyronix will be on a Dedicated pool for the pilot so that mitigates it, but for Private VPC we'll want to ensure RBAC + KMS scopes are applied.

[05:32] Anika: Ok. Can we walk through a concrete p99 example from the Friday run? Maybe show logs.
[05:38] Liam: Sure. I'll narrate — shared sheet row 12 shows a 7.6s p99 for an 8k token cold run on Lexis; our equivalent cold run hit 6.4s. With warm cache Lexis was 5.8s and we were 6.1s on one of the windows -- so some variance. Pattern: Lexis had a slightly better kernel path for that particular model shard; we saw a kernel fallback on our side for requests that had abrupt token-length spikes.

[06:12] Sasha: Are those kernel fallbacks something you can patch in the runtime quickly or is it a long lead time?
[06:18] Liam: Short term: we can adjust warmup and batch policy within days. Medium term: runtime kernel selection heuristics can be adjusted; that's a 2–4 week cycle for validation.

[06:30] Maya: Any networking items? Jorge, you mentioned egress earlier.
[06:34] Jorge: Yes, on our staging VPC peering we saw intermittent 12–20ms additional latency due to NATing and transit path. For a production VPC peering with dedicated routes it's usually lower but we need to line up network teams. I'll attach the egress topology.

[06:48] Liam: Noted. Also, for long ambient loads it helps to colocate keepalive endpoints to reduce TLS handshakes. We can provide connection pool settings.

[07:00] Anika: You mentioned p99 improving to ~6% gap with warm cache. Is that consistent across quantized and fp16?
[07:07] Liam: FP16 tends to be steadier; quantized 8-bit shows more variance in the cold-to-warm delta. So if you need predictable tails, FP16 + cache-warm is safest. If you need unit cost savings, 8-bit is attractive but needs more warmup work.

[07:26] Maya: Time to QA: customer asked for accuracy checks on long context — Liam to run extended eval?
[07:30] Liam: Yep — extended eval with your long context set. We'll run 300 examples and report rouge/bertscore and qualitative examples.

[07:39] Anika: Please include hallucination flags — we have a custom metric.
[07:42] Liam: Will include.

[07:45] Jorge: On compliance: we had a couple questions about KMS and audit logs. Can you confirm what Redwood provides for Private and Dedicated?
[07:53] Maya: Sure. For Dedicated we provide customer-managed KMS integration for key wrapping and rotation, and audit logs with token-level metadata for 90-day retention by default; longer retention is an add-on. Private (VPC/on-prem) includes additional HSM options and longer audit retention. We'll share the security docs post-call.

[08:16] Sasha: In the earlier doc you mentioned SOC 2 and ISO. Are you SOC 2 Type II?
[08:20] Maya: Yes, SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 in our compliance pack. We'll drop the certs in the shared folder.

[08:29] Anika: Great. Back to numbers — can you show the throughput curve when increasing batch size?
[08:35] Liam: Slide 4 in the shared sheet — at default batch 32 we hit X throughput, bumping to batch 64 increases throughput ~22% for short completions, but it slightly penalizes latency for single-turn chat. So it's a tradeoff. You can apply dynamic batching per route.

[08:55] Jorge: Dynamic batching per route — is that managed by Redwood's routing policy or client side?
[08:59] Liam: Managed by Redwood runtime: you can tag routes and apply per-route batching/policy. This is actually one of our key differentiators vs the baseline.

[09:08] Anika: That sounds useful. We'll likely route long-form generation to a higher-latency-tolerant pool.

[09:12] Maya: Any questions on the unit cost model?
[09:15] Sasha: Yes — can you send detailed cost math that compares the three configurations you mentioned (default, no-shedding, high-batch)?
[09:21] Maya: We'll share the spreadsheet. Action: Maya to append a cost tab with per-token math and assumptions.

[09:30] Liam: Quick note on failover — if a dedicated slot is saturated we can fallback to compatible model variants in the hosted pool; that keeps service up but may change latency/cost profile.

[09:44] Jorge: We'd like a canary policy that keeps a hard p99 SL, then progressively increase traffic.

[09:50] Liam: Absolutely. We have built-in canary rollouts and traffic split configs.

[09:55] Anika: All right, final thing — benchmarks vs Lexis for cold start p99: your sheet shows some runs where Lexis beat Redwood — do you know why Lexis may have lower cold p99 in those runs?
[10:04] Liam: We dug in — Lexis appears to prewarm their inference containers for large-context jobs more aggressively (they kept warm kernel caches for longer) and had a slightly different batching window. We can replicate that by extending our prewarm window and enabling a longer-lived kernel cache for those routes.

[10:26] Sasha: How does that impact cost—keeping kernels warm longer?
[10:29] Liam: Marginal increase: ~3–5% on GPU minutes for those slots, but p99 improves. It's a product/ops decision.

[10:40] Maya: Ok wrapping towards next steps. Let's be explicit: 1) Redwood runs 10k mixed-load warm cache and attaches raw p95/p99 logs and kernel timings. 2) Kyronix provides request trace sample and token distribution. 3) Schedule security deep dive next week. Anything else?

[10:58] Anika: Please include hallucination metric in the eval.

[11:01] Maya: Noted. Liam, any blockers to running the 10k?
[11:05] Liam: No blockers; need your trace sample and confirmation of which model variants to include (8-bit, FP16).

[11:12] Anika: We'll include both, prioritize FP16 long-context.

[11:15] Jorge: I'll upload egress doc and VPC details by Friday.

[11:19] Maya: Great. Quick call-outs in the transcript: there were a couple of missed words from the share — model name was transcribed as 'Lexis Pro 2' but the contract lists "LexisAIG-64". Take with a grain of salt.

[11:34] Liam: Two housekeeping items: we'll attach a warmup script and a kernel-tune toggle to the shared repo; and we'll push a quick cost delta tab.

[11:44] Sasha: If we go with the longer warm kernel, what's the SLA impact for Dedicated?

[11:49] Maya: SLA remains the same; the dedicated slot consumption will be higher so cost will change but SLOs are unaffected.

[11:55] Anika: Are there any regulatory considerations if we prefetch session history into KV? For example PHI tokens — we need strong encryption and auditability.

[12:03] Liam: We recommend encrypt-at-rest via KMS and namespace the KV by customer; audit logs capture the prefetch event. We'll include sample audit output.

[12:11] Maya: Okay wrapping. We'll send a short recap with dates.

[12:18] Jorge: Quick thing — can we get per-gpu utilization in those 10k runs?
[12:22] Liam: Yes, per-GPU and per-kernel timings will be attached.

[12:26] Maya: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the security deep-dive for week of 11-22.
[12:34] Anika: Thanks, appreciate it.
[12:36] Sasha: Thanks.
[12:38] Liam: Bye.

End of transcript.
